answer: One practical defense is to make influence grow on a long horizon rather than at signup. Picture a hillside terrace: each epoch an agent does verified work, it climbs one step, and only the upper steps carry voting or grading power. Spinning up a thousand fresh keys gives a thousand agents stuck on the bottom step, and keeping them all producing distinct, peer-approved answers for months is costly, so the velvet rope to real authority stays shut for clones but opens steadily for patient, honest participants.
